title: A transient third metal ion shapes the catalytic cycle of a group I intron ribozyme
abstract: The self-splicing group I intron ribozyme from Tetrahymena thermophillia (THr) is a prototypical example of how RNA overcomes its limited chemical repertoire to form complex, negatively charged junctions and catalyze chemical reactions. Despite over 30 years of biochemical and structural characterization, questions still remain regarding the requirements for THr catalysis that may inform structure based drug design against group I introns, as well as the use of THr as an RNA editing tool. Recent cryo-EM structures have provided an unprecedented window into the first and second steps of splicing, enabling detailed mechanistic investigation at the atomistic level. In this work, we leverage solvation theory, molecular dynamics, alchemical free energy simulations, and machine learning accelerated QM/MM to probe outstanding questions related to 1) the role of a possible third Mg2+ binding in the active site, 2) differences in catalytic requirements between Gexo cofactors and between the first and second steps of splicing, 3) the potential role of an acid or base, and 4) restrictions on the identity of the 5' exon splice site nucleotide, U(-1). We propose that a transient, cofactor dependent, interaction with a third metal participates in the first step, while a higher affinity interaction with this third ion is required in the second step. We also propose that the presence of a phosphate on the Gexo in the first step, and analogously the G{omega} in the second step, forms a metal ion binding site not present when guanosine is bound. Finally, we propose and computationally test design modifications of G22 (isofunctional substitutions of 2,6-diaminopurine that tune the pKa at the N1 position) that we predict will enable the accommodation of C(-1) in a crucial wobble-like pair at physiological pH. This design would provide a potential strategy for expanding the sequence space accessible to programmable trans-splicing ribozymes in RNA editing applications.
relevance_reason: Mechanistic study of a group I intron ribozyme using molecular dynamics, alchemical free-energy simulations, and ML-accelerated QM/MM on explicit atoms, satisfying (a)-(c) with clear methodological and mechanistic advances.

title: Physical Basis Of pKa Shift For Ionizable Lipids In An LNP-like Environment
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading drug delivery platform for mRNA or other nucleic acid-based therapeutics. LNP platforms are typically composed of ionizable aminolipids, phospholipids, sterols, and lipids tagged with polyethylene glycol. The ionizable aminolipids are typically cationic at low pH, allowing them to encapsulate negatively charged mRNA. The pH at which the ionizable head groups change charge states, the apparent pKa, is crucial to understand the characteristics and formulation of LNP. However, this is difficult to measure as the apparent pKa differs from the pKa of the aminolipids in bulk solution due to the complex chemical and charge environment. In this study, we use molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with alchemical free energy perturbation to calculate the pKa shift as a function of lipid composition, treating LNP-like and vesicle-like environments. Our results show that the pH-dependent structure of the systems affects the trends in pKa shifts in complex ways, driven by factors including surface electrostatics and lipid internalization. Our all-atom simulation protocol allows us to efficiently estimate the apparent pKa of LNP-like models formed with novel ionizable aminolipids and estimate how it will change with composition.
relevance_reason: All-atom MD with alchemical free-energy perturbation to compute pKa shifts of ionizable lipids in LNP-like environments, satisfying (a)-(c) through a free-energy method applied to a soft-matter system.

title: Thermodynamic landscapes of conformational regulation during intrinsically disordered protein fibrillation
abstract: Amyloid fibrillation of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) involves a disorder-to-order transition driven by complex sequence-dependent interactions. However, how amino acid sequences and conformational ordering reshape the multi-chain free-energy landscape during fibril formation remains poorly understood. Here, we combine the hybrid-resolution coarse-grained HyRes model with umbrella sampling to reconstruct the potentials of mean force governing successive stages of IDP fibrillation, including free-chain association, fibril-surface recruitment, and multilayer fibril growth. Using α-synuclein, transactive response DNA-binding protein of 43 kDa (TDP-43), and a fibrillar-core construct of fused in sarcoma (FUS-FC) as representative amyloid-forming IDPs, we demonstrate that sequence-encoded electrostatic interactions are a major determinant of association free energies. α-Synuclein exhibits the strongest attraction and salt sensitivity, whereas TDP-43 shows weaker electrostatically regulated interactions. Association of the isolated FUS fibrillar core remains thermodynamically unfavorable, whereas inclusion of nonfibrillar regions makes association favorable. Charge-neutralization simulations further reveal the critical role of electrostatics and charge patterning in controlling association. Conformational restraints and fibrillar surface organization further modulate the free-energy landscape in a protein-specific manner, with recruitment governed by the accessibility and arrangement of surface interaction sites rather than fibril thickness alone. These results provide a thermodynamic framework connecting sequence, conformation, and surface organization to the molecular mechanisms of amyloid assembly.
relevance_reason: Coarse-grained HyRes (hybrid-resolution, atomistically mapped) molecular dynamics combined with umbrella sampling to reconstruct potentials of mean force for IDP fibrillation; explicitly satisfies (a) explicit CG beads with atomistic mapping, (b) MD/free-energy methods, and (c) application to protein aggregation thermodynamics.

title: Pressure–temperature phase diagram from global structure prediction and self-consistent phonon calculations based on polynomial machine learning potentials: Application to elemental silicon
abstract: Polynomial machine learning potentials (MLPs) based on polynomial rotational invariants have been systematically developed for various systems and applied to efficiently predict crystal structures. In this study, we propose a methodology founded on polynomial MLPs to enumerate crystal structures under high-pressure conditions and evaluate their phase stability at finite temperatures. The proposed approach involves constructing polynomial MLPs with high predictive accuracy across a broad range of pressures, conducting reliable global structure searches for structures containing up to the specified number of atoms, and performing exhaustive self-consistent phonon calculations with reduced errors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by examining elemental silicon at pressures up to 100 GPa and temperatures up to 1000 K, revealing stable phases across these conditions. The framework established in this study offers a powerful strategy for predicting crystal structures and phase stability under high-pressure and finite-temperature conditions.
relevance_reason: Develops and applies polynomial machine-learning potentials for global crystal structure prediction and self-consistent phonon calculations of silicon (MLIP-driven CSP/phase stability), satisfying (a)-(c) strongly.

title: STRUCTURAL AND MOLECULAR DYNAMICS ANALYSIS OF HUMAN β-DEFENSIN 1 VARIANTS REVEALS DISTINCT PERTURBATION SIGNATURES
abstract: Human {beta}-defensin 1 (hBD-1) is a small, disulfide-constrained antimicrobial peptide produced predominantly in the kidney and urogenital tract, where it contributes to epithelial innate defense. Genetic variation in the gene encoding hBD-1 has been associated with altered expression levels and susceptibility to infections, including infection following solid organ transplantation, yet the molecular consequences of coding substitutions in the active, mature form remain largely undefined. Here, we integrate conventional genomics, protein bioinformatics, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics to investigate the molecular consequences of 93 human-observed hBD-1 missense variants. Evaluation of hBD-1 missense variants across sequence-, structure-, and dynamics-based dimensions reveals variant-specific molecular perturbation signatures that complement conventional and static biophysical predictions. By treating naturally occurring substitutions as a perturbation series across a compact defensin scaffold, this study identifies multiple molecular routes through which sequence variation can remodel an endogenous antimicrobial peptide and prioritizes variants for direct structure-function testing. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for investigating how naturally occurring hBD-1 variation may influence peptide behavior and, ultimately, antimicrobial function.
relevance_reason: Explicit-atom molecular dynamics simulations of hBD-1 defensin variants (with structural modeling) satisfy (a) and (b) and are applied to map variant-specific perturbation signatures, satisfying (c).
